title: A Door in the Wall
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 33 of 40
content:
The door looked like part of the wall.

I'd seen it every time I went into the garage, but it had been painted the same faded blue as the paneling. It didn't have a handle, just a small latch hidden behind a shelf of spare parts.

Greg found it while looking for a replacement fuse. He stared at the latch for so long I thought he'd forgotten what we'd come to do.

"Oh," he said. "That room."

"What room?"

"The storage room."

"I thought the storage room was the one with the lawn chairs."

"That's the other storage room."

"How many are there?"

"Apparently one more than I remember."

He opened the door. The hinges protested, and a smell of cardboard and damp paper drifted out. We found a stack of boxes, an old suitcase with one broken clasp, and posters rolled into tubes. A small lightbulb hung from a wire near the ceiling, but Greg refused to turn it on until someone had inspected the aged socket.

"Good call," I said, switching on my flashlight.

"See? Responsible adult."

We moved the first box into the clean part of the garage. Greg opened it carefully. Inside were old music flyers, photographs and a letter addressed in handwriting he recognized before he said anything.

His expression changed.

"My parents."

I didn't reach for the letter. "Do you want to read it?"

"I don't know."

"We don't have to decide today."

He laughed once, without humor. "It's been in a box for years. You'd think I'd have made up my mind."

"You're allowed to change your mind more than once."

He sat on the folding stool. I sat on a crate beside him, leaving enough space for him to put the envelope down. The afternoon sun caught dust in the doorway. Somewhere outside, somebody was washing a car with a radio turned up too loud.

He opened the letter eventually. I watched his face, not the words.

"They wanted me to come home," he said. "But only if I was willing to be someone else when I got there."

"Would you like to tell me more?"

He showed me one sentence, then folded the page again. That was all I needed to read.

"I left because I couldn't make them proud without disappearing," he said. "And now I keep thinking maybe I should have been more patient."

"Maybe," I said. "Or maybe you were patient for a long time and leaving was the only thing you knew how to do."

He leaned back against the wall.

"I don't want to hate them forever."

"Then don't promise yourself that you have to. You also don't have to forgive them today."

The smallest box had been pushed behind an old amplifier. Greg picked it up and almost dropped it when the bottom sagged.

"Okay. That's a terrible box."

I fetched a clean one from the garage and helped him move the contents: two concert tickets, a bundle of receipts from places that no longer existed, and a postcard with no message on the back.

"Do you want to keep those?" I asked.

"I don't know. Some of them remind me of good nights. Some remind me of trying too hard to look happy."

"Then we can label them undecided."

He looked at me as though I'd suggested a new form of magic.

"That allowed?"

"It's your storage room."

He grinned briefly. Then he found the family letter beneath the receipts and went quiet again.

I didn't reach for it. There was a difference between helping somebody sort a room and demanding access to every secret hidden in its drawers.

"Would you mind if I put the letter somewhere dry?" he asked.

"Not at all. Do you want me to read it?"

"Not yet."

"All right."

He set it in a clean sleeve and placed it near the top of the box. The rest of the room could stay messy for another afternoon. The wiring still needed a qualified electrician before we used the old outlet.

When we reached the doorway, he looked back.

"I keep thinking you won't understand why I want any of this."

"I don't have to understand every object to respect the person who wants to keep it."

He smiled awkwardly. "That's kind of romantic for a box of bad memories."

"I contain multitudes. Mostly labeled in terrible handwriting."

He laughed, then leaned close enough that his shoulder touched mine.

"I know you have people you loved before me, and people you love now," he said. "You've been honest about ethical non-monogamy and preferring polyamory. I guess I was scared you needed me to prove I was done with my past too."

"You don't. I want you here as you are, not with all the older rooms erased."

He took my hand. We shut the storeroom light off, left the door unlocked for the electrician's scheduled visit, and went to make food. It was enough for today.

We sorted the boxes slowly. Greg kept one absurd poster of himself with a hairstyle so ambitious I had to sit down laughing. He kept a scratched guitar strap and a small photograph of a concert where he'd been happy. He put the family letter into a sealed folder instead of burning it or hanging it above the bed.

I pointed to the broken suitcase.

"Is that trash?"

"I thought so."

He lifted it, found an old train ticket caught in the lining, and changed his mind.

"Maybe it can hold the stuff I'm not ready to decide about."

"That sounds useful."

He looked at me. "You okay with it being here?"

"Why wouldn't I be?"

"Because the room is full of a life you weren't in."

"Greg, I have a life beyond this room too. I've told you I'm ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory. Loving someone doesn't mean acquiring the right to erase everybody who came before or everybody else who's here now."

He considered that, then smiled a little. "I keep forgetting how sensible you are."

"That is a wildly inaccurate description."

"Still." He took my hand. "Thanks for not making me choose between throwing this away and pretending it never hurt."

We carried a few salvageable boxes out to dry and left the wet ones on a plastic sheet for inspection. We didn't store anything against the old electrical outlet. Greg made a note to pay for an electrician before using the room, which was a distinctly unglamorous way to end a discovery.

One of the posters had a name scrawled across the back. Greg saw it and sat down on an upturned crate.

“That's Marty’s handwriting,” he said.

“The manager?”

“Yeah. Old manager. Old mistakes. Probably a little of both.”

He rubbed his thumb across the edge of the cardboard, careful not to smear the ink. For a moment I thought he was going to tell me the entire history. Instead he folded the poster over and tucked it beneath the others.

“You can keep it without explaining it to me,” I said.

“That's kind of the thing,” he answered. “I want to explain some of it. I just don't want it to become a whole trial where I have to prove I was either a great guy or a complete idiot.”

I shifted closer. The room smelled of wet paper, old amplifier dust and motor oil. There was nowhere dignified to sit, so I lowered myself onto the clean part of the floor.

“Maybe you were both,” I said.

He made a face. “Gee, thanks.”

“Not at the same time. Possibly.”

“Better.”

He told me about a night when he'd been sure a bad contract was the only way to get a band on the road, how he'd signed before reading everything because he was afraid of being told no. He didn't blame Rose for the choices he made before he met her, and he didn't turn his old manager into an excuse for everything that followed.

“I wish somebody'd told me I could walk away,” he said.

“Would you have listened?”

“Absolutely not.” He grinned, but it faded. “Maybe later.”

We agreed to photograph the poster before deciding whether to keep it. The photo would be private. Greg didn't owe the wall a shrine, and he didn't owe me the inside of every memory.

As I stood, my hand slipped on the crate. He caught my elbow, then immediately let go when I had my balance.

“Sorry.”

“It's okay. The floor's not my finest dance partner.”

“It's got two left feet,” he said. “And somehow, both of them are mine.”

I laughed, and he laughed too. We left the old papers where they could be sorted on a day when neither of us was tired of being brave.


As evening came, the shadows stretched across the garage. He stood in the doorway with the letter folder in his hand.

"Do you want some company tonight?" I asked.

"Yeah. I do."

We went into the house and made sandwiches. He told me a story about the first poster he'd hung as a teenager, and how he'd been certain it would make him famous. I told him I once kept a ridiculous souvenir because I couldn't bear to admit the trip had been a disappointment. We laughed about being younger and less certain.

He leaned close but stopped.

"Can I kiss you?"

"Yes."

It wasn't a cure for the letter. It wasn't supposed to be. His mouth was warm, his hand a little shaky against my cheek. I moved closer, and he let out a breath he seemed to have been holding for years.

Later, we closed the curtains and let the evening be ours. The storage-room door remained open, its light switched off, with the boxes labeled for another day.

The next morning Greg added a second note to the electrician's list: *Ask before moving stored papers.* He showed it to me without making a speech.

I liked that more than a promise to forget.
